newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour's Brown vows no tax and spend cure-all.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour's Brown vows no tax and spend cure-all.

text.p: Labour's economics spokesman, Gordon Brown, sought on Saturday to ratchet down expectations of his party's left-wingers by ruling out overnight cures for poverty and unemployment if the main opposition party wins Britain's coming election.

Brown, who will become finance minister if opinion polls are right and Labour wins the election, has already promised to freeze income tax rates and keep to the ruling Conservatives' tight spending limits for the next two years.
But in a powerful speech to Labour's Scottish conference, Brown gave a blunt warning that the shape of Britain's finances threatened to tie his hands even more tightly.
"If I told you, 'Vote Labour on Thursday and the money will flow on Friday', none of you would believe me and you would be right.
"Everyone knows you cannot build social justice by creative accounting. You can only build honestly for tomorrow by first facing up to the realities of today," Brown said.

Dwelling on Britain's 26 billion pound ($41 billion) budget deficit, Brown said Labour would not be able to start governing with a "blank sheet" if it wins the election, widely expected to be held on May 1.

"Against this background, what service would I be doing to the people who look to us to provide sustainable public services if I now gloss over the scale of broken Tory promises on spending and borrowing. And if I were to tell you there are huge sums of extra money to spend when everyone knows there are not?" Brown asked rhetorically.

The speech aimed to tackle head on the doubts of many Scottish Labour left-wingers who fear that leader Tony Blair has turned the party into a pale imitation of the Conservatives in his mission to win over wavering middle-class voters.

With public services in Scotland badly strapped for cash and most social and health indicators below the national average, left-wing Labour die-hards would prefer a bold commitment to raise taxes and redistribute wealth.
Brown flatly ruled this out but said Labour could and would make a difference by reordering the priorities of government toward greater fairness.

"I cannot and will not print money or take easy options... but I pledge to this conference we will work tirelessly and unceasingly every day of a Labour government to create the increased wealth we need for the services we want," Brown said.

Brown, who will spearhead Labour's election campaign, said he would make no apology for making its central theme the party's plan to tackle social divisions and the breakdown of community through a welfare-to-work programme financed by a windfall tax on privatised utilities.

With 20 percent of British families of working age having no one in employment, he warned that a fifth consecutive Conservative victory would lead to "the social divisions of a fifth-term underclass".
Brown rejected the argument that an assault on poverty and social divisions would alienate the floating middle-class voters who will determine the election.
"Because poverty and unemployment cost billions and hurts us all, the cause of inner city Britain today is also the cause of middle Britain.
"It is only by preaching the gospel of discontent that we can gain support for our message of national renewal," said Brown, the son of a Scottish preacher. ($1=.6228 Pound)
